about: The words of the chain rorik_850 (Data/encounters/chain_rorik_850_793.json; Design/content/chains/rorik_850.md): Rorik the Dane holds Dorestad from the emperor Lothar from 850, a heathen lord over a Christian port, and a merchant must be his man or not. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the news items the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: the count is Rorik (the spine's cast.rorik, historical), the toll man Eystein (cast.eystein, invented), the bishop Hunger of Utrecht (historical); Thiadward, the priest Adalger and Hiddo of the coast are ordinary invented people. Nothing here is quoted from a translation: what the annals of Fulda and of Saint-Bertin and Flodoard say is given in our own plain words. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: The Dane at the dam
Nine long ships lie along the upper bank with their masts down. The man at the toll house has a tally stick in his belt and an arm ring above it, and he is not a Frisian.
Eystein. I take the toll now. Your house's name, your mark, and what is in the boat. I learned your tongue here as a boy, so say it at your own speed.
The king's tenth, as before. It goes into the same chest. The chest goes to a different hall, and from there to the emperor, less the keeping of nine ships.
Last spring those nine ships burned every barn between here and the Waal. This summer they are the count's fleet. The emperor could not beat him, so he hired him. I am told this is statecraft.
My lord is sworn to keep other Danes off this river. He will. He knows how they think, where they water and what they are afraid of. He is what they are afraid of.
Some houses are going round by the Waal so as not to pay a heathen. It is a day longer and the king's man at Noviomagus takes his tenth just the same. But he is baptised, so it feels lighter.
Give him your name and your house's mark, and ask for your father's place at the dam
Ask him plainly what the emperor has granted, and for how long
Tell him nothing, and tell Thiadward you will go round by the Waal next time

Eystein cuts your mark into his stick beside your father's place, which he has from the old toll man's stick. He takes half toll from you for a month. He says his lord wants the old houses to stay, and that this is what wanting costs.

He answers without offence. Dorestad and the counties about it, from the emperor's own hand, on two conditions: the dues paid in honestly, and other Danes kept out. For how long? For as long as both are done. He says it is the same lease any count has, with more rowing.

Eystein writes nothing on his stick and looks at the gap for a moment. Thiadward walks you back to the boat. He says the Waal is a day longer, and that he would go that way himself if his storehouse could be put in a boat.
Hands between hands
The count holds court in the old toll hall. The free men of the bank are called in by name, house by house, and yours is the next.
Your house. Come to the front, stand where the mat is, and do not look at the dogs. He will speak Frankish. He speaks it better than the last count did.

I am Rorik. I hold this place of the emperor and I have sworn to him. Now the free men swear to me, as they did to my brother and me in the old emperor's day. A man who is mine, I answer for. On this river and on the sea.
You are the one who was going round by the Waal. And here you are at my door. A merchant goes where the market is. I have always liked that in merchants.

The oath to the emperor is every free man's. But this is hands between hands. A Christian should think before he puts his hands inside a heathen's, and thinks again before he does it in front of his priest.
Your priest keeps his church because my men stand on the bank. I have not asked him to love me for it. I ask nobody for that. It is not in the grant.
I have this church's relics here in their box. Swear the emperor's peace on them, as your father did, and let the Dane make what he can of it.
Put your hands between his and be his man
Swear the emperor's peace on the priest's relics, as your father did, and put your hands in no man's
Swear nothing: you pay the tenth, and that is all a toll is owed

His hands are dry and hard and he holds yours a breath longer than the words need. Half toll for a year, and a bench at his table at the feasts, his and yours both. Adalger the priest finds something to look at in the roof.

You swear on the box. The count laughs, not unkindly. Then you and he serve the same lord, he says, and of the two of you he is the one with the ships. He has your name kept among the emperor's men. The priest nods to you on the way out.
Nobody is angry. The count says a toll is owed a tenth and he will see that he gets it. Eystein cuts your mark on a second stick, a short one. You do not ask what the short one is for.
Light pennies
The count's steward counts ninety-six pennies onto your hatch for what the hall has had of you. They are new, they carry the emperor's name, and they ring wrong on the board.
Ninety-six. Eight shillings, as agreed. New from the mint this month, with the emperor's name on every one. Count them again if it pleases you. It is the same number each time.
I strike what I am given to strike. I was given the emperor's name and a bar of silver that was not all silver. The name is very good work. I will say that for the name.
You are my lord's man. Between his men a penny is a penny.
You are the emperor's man, I hear. Then you will not refuse the emperor's coin.
My scale is on the bench. It tells the truth to anyone, which is why nobody thanks it.
Take them by tale and say nothing
Ask the moneyer for his scale and be paid by weight
Leave the pennies and take the debt in furs from the fleet's store

Ninety-six by count. On any scale they are seventy-two, and north of the Eider nobody takes a penny by count. The steward marks that you did not make him say it twice, and has Eystein take half toll from you for two months.

The moneyer weighs them without a word. A quarter short. The steward shrugs, opens a bag of cut silver from the north and drops pieces in the pan until it sits level. He says his lord pays his debts in whatever a man can carry.

The steward puts his hand flat on the pan before the weight goes in. The emperor's name is on them, he says. Do you doubt the emperor? There are a good many men in the hall. You take the ninety-six by count.

He sweeps the pennies back into the bag and sends a boy for a timber of marten: forty skins, winter pelts, tied in the northern way. The fleet's store is full of them. They will be cheap on this bank until it is not.
Two kings' sons go north
The long ships are in the water and being stored. Word came in the winter that the king of the Danes is dead with most of his kin, and the count is of that kin.
The king is dead and so are his nephews, all in one battle. They have made a boy king because he was what was left. My kinsman Godfrid and I are going to look at this boy.
Nine ships, forty men to a ship, and I will not have them stop to rob farms on the way: it is slow, and they are my farms. I need bread that keeps. Who on this bank can find it by the new moon?
He was hired to keep the river. Now the river's keeper is going to be a king somewhere else. If he wins we have no count. If he loses we have an angry one.

The emperor has given all Frisia to his son, the young Lothar. A young king likes to be asked things. Six houses are putting their marks to a word for him: who keeps the river while the count is away? Yours would make seven.
You are my man. If I come back a king, I will need a merchant who knows the way to my hall. If I come back as I am, I will need bread again.
Take his order: thirty sacks of ship's bread on the bank within thirty days
Put your mark with Thiadward's on a word to the young king: who keeps the river while the count is away?
Wish him a fair wind and keep to your own trade
Thirty sacks, at close to twice what bread fetches. The steward does not haggle. A fleet does not haggle in the week before it sails. Bring it within thirty days, to the upper bank.

A clerk of the church writes it on a leaf: seven marks and a cross. Nobody tells the count. Thiadward says that is not the same as the count not knowing, and that he would rather be known for asking the king than for keeping quiet.
The count thanks you for the wind as gravely as if you had it to give. Every oven on the bank is baking for the ships. Bread and ale will be dear at Dorestad until they are gone.
The fleet goes to the Eider
The count is taking his ships north again, this time with the king's leave and a promise of land by the Eider. He leaves the toll man, twelve men and one ship that leaks.

The boy king of the Danes has offered me the land between the sea and the Eider, and my lord King Lothar says I may go and take it. Two kings agreeing is rare. I mean to be there before either thinks again.
I am left with twelve men, one ship and a bailing scoop. If anyone asks, the count is hunting and will be back for supper.
Every skipper between here and Ripa knows by now that the river has no keeper this summer. News like that needs no wind.
My men will be a summer on a bare shore with silver and nothing to spend it on. Bring cloth and wine to Sliesthorp before Saint John's feast and you will not carry any of it home.
My grandfather put the house's silver in the ground in the year of the first fleet and dug it up again in the autumn. I know which post. I am telling you only that it can be done.
Sail north in the fleet's wake with cloth and wine: his men will need both
Stay with the house, and put its silver in the ground behind the storehouse
Take the boat up the river and trade above Noviomagus until he is home

He names the place: the market at the head of the Slie, before Saint John's feast. Cloth and wine will be dear there as long as his men lie by the Eider. He says to come round by the coast and not through the mouths at night.
A pot, under the third post from the water, on a night without a moon. You hear a spade in Thiadward's yard as you tread the earth flat. In the morning you each ask how the other slept.
You tell Eystein you have business up the river. He says he would have business up the river too, if he were not the one who was left. He does not say it as a reproach. He helps you cast off.
Between the sea and the Eider
The count sits on a sea chest at the head of the Slie, selling what a kingdom's edge gives: furs, amber and promises. He greets you in Frisian so that his own men will not follow it.
My merchant. You came by the coast, as I said. Sit. Here I am not a count. Here I am a kinsman with ships, which is a harder trade, and worse paid.
I have the land between the sea and the Eider. It is mostly sea. The boy king was glad to give it to me: it lies between him and the Franks, and so now do I.

The church here was shut after the old king fell. It is open again, and the young king lets us ring a bell. A Dorestad man may hear Mass at the Slie. Tell them that at home. They did not believe it of the last bell either.
You are from the Rhine? I passed forty sail off the islands after midsummer, standing south. Not his. I asked whose, and they asked who wanted to know, so I did not want to know.
Forty. And I left Eystein twelve men. Well. A town can be built again in a year. I have seen it done. I have also seen why it needed doing.
Buy under his peace: a timber of marten and four sacks of amber for 110 d
Ask him for a token his ships will know
Hear the skipper out, buy nothing, and turn for home on the next wind

Forty winter martens and four sacks of amber off the western beaches, for less than half what the Rhine pays. His steward counts in his own tongue, slowly, for your sake. By the last sack you can count to forty in it.

He looks at you a while, then cuts a hand's length from a silver arm ring and scratches three strokes in it with his knife. Hang it at the stem, he says. Any ship of his kin will know it. He does not say what the others will do.
You buy the skipper ale and hear it all twice. Forty sail, standing for the Rhine mouths, a fortnight ago. Whatever they went to do is done. You load water and wait for a wind with north in it.
The other Danes
There are sails below the town that are not the count's. They have been counted three times from the church roof and the number has grown each time.
Not ours. Ours come home in a line and singing. Those are spread across the whole river like a net.
A church can be built again. I have two gospel books, a psalter, the altar silver and three clerks, and none of those can. I need a boat that goes upstream, and I need it before the tide helps them.

The upper dam is narrow and staked. Thirty men could hold it against three boats at a time, if they stayed. I have nineteen who say they will stay. Eystein's twelve make thirty-one. I am one short of comfortable.
The bishop has gone inland with what could be carried in a day. What could not be carried in a day is on this bank, with me. Daventre, he said. Saint Lebuin's, on the IJssel.
You are back from up the river. You have a gift for arriving. Stay this time, or go at once: there is no room on the bank for a man who is thinking about it.

There is a third way and I am ashamed to know it. Their chief sells peace by the house. Five shillings, and a shield goes up on your door post. It works. I have hung those shields myself, in other towns.
Take the priest, his clerks and the church's books up the river to Daventre
Stand at the dam head with Eystein's twelve and the Frisian houses
Row out to their chief and buy your own storehouse free (60 d)

Three clerks, a priest and a chest that takes four men to lift. One clerk reads the psalms aloud the whole way, against fear, and by the IJssel you can follow the short ones. At Daventre the bishop's steward pays the freight: ten shillings, counted twice.

They try the upper dam at dusk, three boats abreast, and the first one opens herself on the stakes. After that they go looking for softer houses, and find them. The dam's houses stand. In the morning they make up a purse for those who stood on it.

The dam is held until dark and lost in the dark. You get the boat off with a cut hand aboard and smoke behind you. Half the bank burns. The men who were on the dam with you do not forget who else was there.

Their chief takes five shillings, bites one penny, laughs at it, and takes them anyway. A shield hangs on your door post while your neighbours' roofs burn. Your storehouse stands. There will be no wine on this bank until new ships come down.
The count comes home
The lower bank is black posts and new planks. The count's ships are back along the upper bank, and the men of the houses stand in the road with their arms folded.
We paid a tenth to a man who was sworn to keep pirates off the river. The pirates came. The man was away getting himself a second country. I ask only what the tenth was for.

It was for the summers in which this bank did not burn. Count them. Before me it burned most years. I went away for one summer with my king's leave, and you have learned what I am worth. I did not plan the lesson. I will not waste it.
This one stood on the dam with me, lord. I say it here, in the road, so that both sides hear it.
This one came north with cloth when I asked. He was where I told him to be. I ask you all how many men that is true of.

The young king is at Noviomagus for the winter. We have a leaf written: let the king send a count of his own people, with horsemen. Somebody with a boat must carry it. None of us wants to be seen going.

I have broken up two ships that were past mending. Oak, seasoned, free to any house that builds on its old plot before Saint Martin's feast. And half toll for a season to those who do. A burned town pays no tenth at all. I can reckon that much.
Speak for him in the road: he came back, and no Frankish count ever did
Carry the houses' complaint to the king's palace at Noviomagus
Say nothing for either, take his ship timber and mend your own dam head

You say it: in all the years of fleets, which Frankish count came back to a burned bank with timber? Nobody answers, and they go home muttering. That evening the steward brings ten shillings in old pennies, the heavy kind. He says his lord noticed which kind.

The houses pay your carriage. At the palace a clerk takes the leaf, reads it twice, and asks whether the Dane has paid in the dues. He has. Then the king, says the clerk, has no other fleet to send. He keeps the leaf. Kings keep everything.

Ship's oak makes good posts. It has already learned about water. You are a fortnight at it, and you say nothing for anyone. Eystein takes half toll from every house that built, until Saint Martin's feast comes round again.
The bishop without a church
The bishop of Utrecht has no Utrecht. He keeps his household in borrowed rooms, and he has asked for any merchant who lies at Dorestad and knows the Dane.
The bishop lodges here by Saint Lebuin's until the king finds him a house. Wipe your feet. The floor is borrowed too.
The bishop is here for three days to see what is left of his church. It is the wall on your right. Yes, that one.
I am Hunger, and I am told the name suits a bishop with no see. You lie at Dorestad. You have seen this Rorik eat, deal and lose his temper. Tell me: is he a man who could be brought to the water?
They say your hands have been between his. I do not ask you to repent of it today. I ask you to use it.
You brought my priest and my books out when the fleet came. I have not forgotten. I am asking you because of it.
I have written to him. With the letter goes a length of white linen, enough for a robe. He will know what it is for. They always do. It is the letter they have read to them twice.
Carry the bishop's letter and the white cloth to the count
Carry nothing, but tell the bishop what the Dane wants: his toll untouched, and a king who cannot unseat him
Say you carry cloth and wine, and that souls are another man's freight

Thirty pennies for the carriage. The clerk reads you the letter twice, in Latin and then in Frisian, so that you can say it if the leaf is lost. It is shorter than you expected. It offers the count a bishop's good word with two kings, and heaven after.

You tell him. The Dane wants his toll left alone and a lord who cannot take the grant back. The bishop listens to the end. Men have come to the water for less, he says, and has the clerk write down what you said, in your own words.

The bishop says that souls are everyone's freight, and that he has noticed merchants prefer the kind that can be weighed. The clerk shows you out. On the stair he says the household has no wax for its altar, and would pay over the price.
The white robe
A tub has been set in the largest church on the bank and filled from the river. The count stands beside it in his shirt, and half his men stand outside with their backs to the door.
He is asked three times if he forsakes the devil and all his works, and three times he says he does. He says it in good Frankish. I have known Franks who put less into it.
You carried the letter and the cloth. So you will stand where I can see you. If the roof falls on me, I want one man there who can tell them it was not my idea.
A merchant. Good. You people understand a bargain, and you can tell the others it was a fair one. Stand where you like.
I wear the cross for the day's business and the hammer for the night's. My lord has decided to wear one of them all day. A count can afford to be simple.

They tell of a man at the old emperor's court who was baptised every Easter for the white robe. One year the linen was poor and he said so. Twenty times washed, he said, and never such a sack. My lord has had the cloth looked at first.
Stand among the witnesses and give wax for the candles (40 d)
Stand at the back with Eystein and ask what a white robe is worth on this river
Stay outside with the men who will not go in, and stand them ale

He goes under three times and comes up blowing like a seal. The first thing he does is look round to see who is there. Your candles burn the whole Mass. Eystein takes half toll from the witnesses for half a year, and calls it a christening gift.

Eystein reckons it up, in Frisian and then in Danish where Frisian lacks the word. A bishop's good word with two kings. An oath that Christians have to keep back. A dry grave. Against that, a wet shirt and some sour faces at home. He calls it cheap.

You stand ale to the men at the door. They say their lord has not changed lords, only taken on one more, and that he was always good at holding of several. Your own crew think better of you for the ale. The priest saw where you stood.
The flood winter
The river is over the lower bank and into the fields behind. A fisherman from the mouths has counted more sails than the count has, and the houses are loading carts for a great estate inland.
We are going to the big estate behind the fields, all the houses, with what the carts will take. It has a ditch and a stone barn, and it is an hour from any river. Ships do not go where carts go.
The fisherman says sixty. Halve what a fisherman says and it is still thirty, and my lord has nine. I can do sums. It is what I am kept for.
Look at the fields. That was a road at Christmas. I could take a ship over it now and not touch. I am not saying where I would take her. I am saying I could.
You have stood with the houses before. If you have something to say against the carts, they will hear you. They may not do it. But they will hear you.
You are the Dane's man. If you tell the houses to get into boats, half of them will ask whose boats, and where the boats are going.
I know whose sails they are. Two of them have eaten at my table. That is worth something, and it is not worth a town. Do not ask me yet which it is worth.
Tell the houses the flood is a road for ships, and take all who will come by boat up the IJssel to Daventre
Go to the count as his man and ask him to put his ships across the river
Take your own boat into the reeds above the town, and watch

You take Thiadward to the edge of the fields and push an oar down: a man's height of water over the cart road. He looks at it a long time. By dusk eleven boats are strung out against a brown river, yours ahead with a lantern. Six houses are on the IJssel before the sails reach the town.

They argue until the light goes. A cart is a thing a man can see the wheels of. You take off two families and a clerk in your own boat, low in the water, and row all night. The carts go inland without you.

He hears you out. Nine ships do not stop sixty, he says; they only choose where to sink. He will talk to them instead. It is cheaper, and some of them owe him. Then he tells you to have your boat above the town by dark, and does not say why.

From the reeds you see the toll chest carried aboard the count's ship, two days before any sail shows. You see the sails come. You see his nine ships lie still at the upper bank while the lower burns. On the second night there is another fire, inland, where the carts went.
On Rorik's advice
The fleet went up the river as far as the island below Neuss and came down again, on the count's advice, they say. Dorestad is ash to the upper bank. Now everyone reckons what he is owed and by whom.

The king came up on one bank and the Saxons on the other, and my lord went between and told the fleet what he would do in their place. They did it. They went home. That is the whole of it, and nobody likes it for being so short.

They found the estate, you know. Over the fields, as you said. The stone barn is full of ash and other men's dead. We should have been in it. Six houses know whose lantern they followed. We have talked, and we have something to put to you.
You took off two families when the rest would not listen. They are alive. I was asked to tell you that the rest of us know it now. Those of the rest who are left.
They went to the estate with the carts. The ships went over the fields after them. Thiadward's house is his widow and a boy now. I buried eleven men I had bought and sold with for twenty years.

You kept your oath in a winter when it was easier not to. I still have my counties, and I mean to have men in them I can name. Nine hundred in old coin, a ship off my own bank, and my mark for her stem. Take it now. I am generous while I am relieved.
You are not my man. So I owe you nothing, and you owe me nothing, and each of us may say what he likes about that winter. I would think for a time before I said it.
Settle the houses you brought out on the IJssel bank, and swear fellowship with them
Take what the count gives the men who kept their oath
Take nothing yet: there are dead to bury, and it is not yet clear whose silver this is

Six houses put a share each into one chest and swear on Saint Lebuin's altar to stand for one another's debts and dead. They mark you the first plot above the landing at Daventre. Thiadward will sail a second boat under your mark. Dorestad's names are on a new bank, and none of them is on a grave.

Nine hundred pennies of the old weight. A Danish-built ship, broad, with a mast that lowers, off his own bank. And three strokes cut in her stem: no ship of his kin will lay you aboard. As you leave the hall the bishop's clerk is at the door, writing names.

You help carry what was found at the estate to the churchyard, and pay for the candles. It takes four days. On the last the bishop's clerk asks where your boat will lie this spring. He writes the answer down.
What the bishop asks
The bishop has a letter from the archbishop of Reims open on the table, and a list of every house that lay at Dorestad in the flood winter. Yours is on it.

From Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, to my lord. If it was by Rorik's counsel that the heathen did what they did, my lord is to lay a fitting penance on him. There is a second letter, to Rorik himself. That one we have not seen. We can guess its temper.

He is baptised. So he is mine to judge, as he never was while he was a heathen. I think nobody explained that to him at the tub. You were at Dorestad that winter. What did you see, and what will you swear to?
You are his sworn man. An oath to a lord does not bind a man to lie to his bishop. I say that as the law has it. I know it is easier to say in this room than on that river.
You have carried for this church before, and you were not paid what it was worth. I remember my debts. It is a habit I have had time to form, lately.
I do not want his counties. The kings may weigh those. I want him at a church door in Lent, where the widows can see him. No lord of that river has stood there yet. One should.
Tell all of it: what you saw, what he said before the sails came, and swear to it
Say only what every man knows: he talked the fleet away, and he talked too late for the dead
Say you saw nothing a man could swear to

You tell it in order and swear on Saint Martin's cloth. The bishop sets the penance. The count stands a Lent at the church door in his shirt, and pays the toll of that winter back to the houses of the dead. He does it. Your share and the bishop's thanks come to eleven hundred pennies. Saint Martin's bank is free to your house, and you are written down as the saint's man.

It is enough for a lesser penance: a fast, and alms to the widows by the bishop's hand. The count pays without a word. The bishop gives your house Saint Martin's bank free of toll, and seven hundred pennies for handling the alms honestly. Eystein, at the next toll, counts your cargo twice.
The bishop looks at you for some time and then at the clerk. The clerk draws a line under your house's name: not through it, and not round it. You are thanked for coming. Nobody sees you to the door.
The Cokingi
The men of the coast have risen against the Dane. They carry eel spears and old swords, they have a name nobody has heard before, and both sides want a boat.

I am Hiddo. I speak for the districts. We paid the Dane a tenth to keep Danes off, and buried our kin anyway. We have told him the lease is up. He is on the wrong side of the water and collecting ships.

I am Hiddo. We put the Dane out three summers ago. Now a king has met him at Noviomagus and made a treaty, and he is to be our count again, by a king we never chose. We are not finished. Neither, it seems, is he.
Your house's mark was on the leaf that went to the king, years back. The king did nothing. We remembered who asked. That is why I come to your boat first.

Two women, a boy, a chest and me. That is all of the count's household on this bank, and the men with eel spears know which house it is in. I need a boat tonight. I never asked a Frisian for anything but the tenth before.
Word from the count, by a fisherman: You are my man still. Bring my household off, and bring the chest. I am coming back with ships, and I will know who carried and who watched.
Word from the count, by a fisherman: You were never my man, and I never burned your house. Stay out of the way of this and you will find the toll no higher when I am back.
Carry the Cokingi's bread and their word along the coast
Take the count's household and his chest off the bank in your boat, as his man
Be nobody's man: sell bread to both, and move your goods to Daventre

Three weeks from terp to terp with bread and one sentence: the day, and the place. By harvest the Dane is off the coast. The districts pay you in cloth and in the toll they did not send him. A pilot of the Vlie takes you out and shows you his marks, the church, the dune and the two withies. He says it is not done, and that his father would have drowned him for it.

Two women, a boy, Eystein and an iron-bound chest, down the river in the dark with muffled oars. The count pays from the chest when he is back with ships, and he is back: thirteen hundred pennies, a ship from his bank, his mark on her stem. On the coast they do not sell to your house for a generation.

A rising eats as much as a fleet and pays sooner. Six hundred pennies in one summer, from both sides, and neither thanks you. A cousin of Thiadward's house takes your goods into his storehouse on the IJssel, where neither side comes, and will keep them there for a share.

This year the emperor Lothar received Rorik the Dane into his fealty and gave him Dorestad and other counties, on his oath to pay in the king's dues and to keep the pirates of the Danes off the river.
This year Rorik, who rules in Dorestad, went with his fleet to the Eider with King Lothar's leave. After midsummer forty sail that were not his were seen standing for the Rhine mouths.
This year in the flood winter the heathen men burned Dorestad and a great estate behind it. The houses of the bank had gone by boat up the IJssel beforehand, and they have taken plots at Daventre.
This year the fleet that burned Dorestad went up the Rhine as far as Neuss and came down again on the advice of Rorik. He keeps his counties, and has rewarded the men who held to him.
This year Rorik the Northman, being baptised, did penance at the word of Hunger, bishop of Utrecht, for the winter in which Dorestad was burned. Merchants who were there bore witness.
This year the men of the coast, who are called by a new name Cokingi, drove Rorik out of Frisia. King Lothar has called out his host, for it is said that Rorik will come again with Danes.
This year there was fighting in Frisia between the people of the land and Rorik the Dane. Houses that were of Dorestad are moving their goods to Daventre on the IJssel.

A grey summer morning at Dorestad's upper dam: a fair Dane in his thirties with a moustache, a Frankish cloak over a northern tunic, a silver arm ring and a tally stick, stands at the toll house door; behind him nine long ships lie along the bank with their masts lowered, and a Frisian merchant in a short cloak watches from a plank road.

Inside a timber hall by firelight, afternoon: a tall fair man of about forty in a Frankish count's cloak and sword belt, gold rings on his arms, sits on a bench holding out his open hands; a Frisian merchant stands before him on a rush mat; to one side a tonsured priest holds a small relic box, and two hounds lie by the hearth.

Midday on a jetty at Dorestad, flat light: a heavy Danish steward tips a row of thin new pennies onto the hatch of a small boat; a Frankish moneyer in a leather apron stands by with a folding balance in his hand, looking at the sky; one penny is on edge, spinning.

A windy spring day on the upper bank: nine long ships afloat, men passing sacks and casks aboard down a line; in front the count, bare-headed, one foot on a gunwale, speaks with two merchants; smoke from many bread ovens blows across the town behind.

Early morning, clear and cold: the count's fleet rowing away down the river in a line, small; in front, on an empty bank, the toll man stands with a bailing scoop in his hand beside one old ship drawn up on rollers, and a Frisian merchant beside him looks the other way, up the river.

A long northern evening at the head of the Slie: the count sits on a sea chest on a shingle strand, bundles of marten skins and sacks of amber at his feet, ships drawn up behind; a Danish skipper leans in to speak; far back, a small wooden church with a bell hung in a frame beside it.

Dusk at Dorestad, the sky red down the river: many sails spread across the water below the town; in front a priest and three clerks carry a heavy chest and books down a jetty to a small boat, while behind them armed Frisians and a dozen Danes crowd onto a narrow staked dam.

A raw autumn day: black burned posts along the lower bank and stacks of pale new planks; the count, in a travelling cloak, stands in a plank road facing a knot of Frisian merchants with folded arms; behind him men are breaking up an old ship for her oak.

A bare borrowed room in winter light from a small window: a lean bishop of about fifty in a plain dark cloak, a wooden staff against the wall, sits at a trestle with a folded letter and a length of white linen on it; a young clerk stands with a wax tablet; a merchant waits by the door with his cap in his hand.

Inside a timber church, candles and daylight from the open door: a big fair man of fifty stands in his shirt beside a large wooden tub of water, a priest with a raised hand before him; a folded white robe lies on a bench; through the door, the backs of armed Danes who will not come in.

A dark winter afternoon, rain: the river spread wide over fields, fence tops and a cart road going down into brown water; on the last dry ground Frisian families load ox carts; in front a merchant pushes an oar down into the flood to show its depth, and a lantern burns in a small boat beside him.

A pale early spring morning on a river bank: in the far distance a burned town, only posts standing; in front the count at a board on trestles with an open chest of pennies, the toll man beside him; to the other side a group of Frisian merchants waits apart, and a clerk stands by a door with a tablet.

A stone-walled room, a single candle though it is day: the bishop, older now and thin, sits with an open letter and a long list before him; the clerk points to one line with a pen; a merchant stands with his hand laid on a small relic box.

Late summer evening on a Frisian shore, long shadows: a crowd of coast men with eel spears and old swords around a grey-bearded spokesman on a terp; below them at the water a small boat, and beside it the ageing toll man with two cloaked women, a boy and an iron-bound chest, waiting to see which way the skipper turns.

The ending 'the count's man': a broad Danish-built ship on a river in clear morning light, three strokes cut in her stem, a Frisian skipper at the steering oar; on the bank behind, the count raises one hand, and further back a clerk writes.

The ending 'the houses brought out': a new plank landing on the IJssel at Daventre in summer, six house frames going up in a row, a church behind; in front Frisian merchants and their wives stand round one chest with their hands on it.

The ending 'the bishop's witness': a church door in Lent, grey light; a big fair man in a plain shirt, bare-headed and bare-footed, stands beside it while widows in dark head-cloths go in past him; the bishop watches from inside; a merchant stands at the edge of the yard.

The ending 'the coast's man': a small boat in the Vlie at low water, evening; a Frisian pilot stands in the bow pointing at a far church, a dune and two withies in line; behind, on a terp, fires burn and no long ship lies anywhere on the water.

The ending 'nobody's man': a storehouse door at Daventre, a man barring it from inside on stacked bales and casks; outside on the river, small in the distance, a long ship and a crowd on a bank face one another, and a loaded boat rows away from both.
